title: The Best Listening Strategy In The World
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin uses a personal anecdote — a class he loved that fell apart under a new teacher, then instantly snapped back into order the moment he took over — to argue that the single most powerful listening strategy is follow-through. He contends that most teachers believe they are consistent and hold students accountable for every act of misbehavior, but in practice their boundaries are movable, negotiable, and governed by mood rather than fixed principle. Teachers, he argues, act more like judges deciding case-by-case whether to enforce consequences than like referees who call violations the same way every time. Persuading, lecturing, bargaining, and making 'executive decisions' to let students off the hook all masquerade as accountability but actually erode it. What restored order instantly in his former students was not a special technique but a reputation, built over months, for doing exactly what he said he would do. He concludes that words only carry authority when backed by a consistent history of follow-through.
points: A reputation for consistent follow-through, not any clever technique, is what makes students listen and comply.
Most teachers believe they are consistent but in practice apply boundaries that are movable and mood-dependent.
Effective teachers act like referees who call violations the same way every time, not judges who decide case-by-case.
Persuading, lecturing, bargaining, and letting students off the hook all masquerade as accountability while undermining it.
A class's behavior can flip dramatically within minutes depending solely on whether the adult in charge has a track record of enforcing what they say.
quotes: The hard truth is that most teachers believe they’re consistent but they’re not. They believe they hold students accountable for every act of misbehavior—and will swear to you they do—but they don’t.

There is a great disconnect between perception and reality when it comes to classroom management. A huge swath of teachers will tell you that there is one boundary for all students in their classroom.
Not even close. They’re judges who decide to hold students accountable (or not) based on their mood, their fears, the time of day, the severity of the misbehavior, and who is doing the misbehaving.
I had a reputation for doing what I said. It was a sure thing they could take to the bank, and this makes all the difference.
The big and great powerful listening strategy is follow through .
